entry: Chronic autoimmune disorder causing loss of skin pigment in patches. The patches, which often grow and change shape, are most prominent on the face, hands and wrists, and they can appear anywhere on the body. Changes in the immune system and potential genetic factors are thought to be involved, and triggers may include sun or chemical exposure, stress and physical trauma. In antiquity it was often confused with [[Leprosy|leprosy]]. Treatments include topical immunosuppressants and [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light therapy. It is neither contagious nor life-threatening, but stigma can lead to depression. [[Michael Jackson]] was among those who had it.

Drawing by [[Leonardo da Vinci]] of a nude man in two overlapping positions, inscribed in a [[Circle|circle]] and a [[Square|square]]. Dated to c. 1490, it illustrates ideal human proportions and was inspired by the Roman architect [[Vitruvius]]. The drawing is executed in pen, ink and metalpoint on paper measuring 34.4 cm × 25.5 cm, and it shows meticulous preparation with calipers and compass. Acquired in 1822 by the Gallerie dell'Accademia in [[Venice]], it is rarely displayed because of its fragility.

Roman architect and military engineer, author of the treatise *De architectura*. It is the only surviving treatise on architecture from antiquity and has been regarded since the [[Renaissance]] as the first book on architectural theory. Vitruvius states that buildings should have three attributes: *firmitas*, *utilitas* and *venustas* ("strength", "utility" and "beauty"). He served in the Roman army as an artilleryman, specializing in the construction of [[Ballista|ballistae]] and other war machines, and may have served with [[Julius Caesar]]'s chief engineer. The treatise was dedicated to [[Augustus]] and was widely copied in the Middle Ages. It was rediscovered in 1414, and [[Leon Battista Alberti]] published it in *De re aedificatoria* (c. 1450). Its discussion of perfect proportion inspired Leonardo da Vinci's drawing of the [[Vitruvian Man]].

Italian film director and [[Actor|actor]], a leading figure of the neorealist movement. He began his career as a [[Theatre|theater]] actor before turning to directing. His films *Sciuscià* and [[Bicycle Thieves]] won honorary Academy Awards, and *Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow* and *Il giardino dei Finzi Contini* won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. *Bicycle Thieves* was deemed the greatest film of all time in *Sight & Sound* magazine's 1952 poll of filmmakers and critics. De Sica was nominated for Best Supporting Actor for his role in Charles Vidor's 1957 adaptation of [[Ernest Hemingway]]'s *A Farewell to Arms*, in which his acting was considered the highlight.

Danish-born Russian naval officer and explorer. Bering entered the navy of Tsar [[Peter the Great]] in 1704 and served in the [[Great Northern War]]. He led the First Kamchatka Expedition (1725–1730), which confirmed that Asia and North America are separated, and later led the Great Northern Expedition, which explored the [[Aleutian Islands]] and the Alaskan coast. The [[Bering Strait]], the [[Bering Sea]] and Bering Island were named in his honor. He died of [[Scurvy|scurvy]] on Bering Island, and his surviving crew returned to Kamchatka with maps that helped pave the way for Russian colonization of [[Alaska]]. Russia sold the territory to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million.

Family of small to medium-sized feliform [[Mammal|mammals]], comprising 14 genera and 33 species. John Edward Gray named and first described the family in 1821. Its members, including civets, genets and palm civets, occur throughout [[Africa]], southern Europe, and South and [[Southeast Asia]]. Viverrids are the most primitive of the feliform families and are less specialized than the [[Felidae]]. A pouch or gland occurs beneath the anus, and most species have a penis bone.

British stage and screen actress, known for her Academy Award-winning roles. Leigh won Best Actress Academy Awards for Scarlett O'Hara in *Gone with the Wind* (1939) and for Blanche DuBois in the film adaptation of *A Streetcar Named Desire* (1951). She also won a Tony Award for the Broadway musical *Tovarich* (1963). Primarily a stage performer, she played roles ranging from the heroines of [[George Bernard Shaw]] comedies to Shakespearean characters such as Ophelia, Cleopatra and Lady Macbeth. In 1999 the American Film Institute ranked her 16th-greatest female movie star of classic Hollywood cinema. She was married to [[Laurence Olivier]] from 1940 to 1960, and they appeared together in many stage productions. Leigh had recurrent bouts of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], which ultimately contributed to her death.

Voivode of [[Wallachia]] in three separate reigns (1448, 1456–1462 and 1476). Vlad sought to strengthen central authority and resisted the expansion of the [[Ottoman Empire]]. In 1462 he attacked Ottoman territory and attempted a night attack to capture Sultan [[Mehmed II]] at Târgoviște. Known for impaling his enemies, including Saxon villagers and the sultan's envoys, he was imprisoned by [[Matthias Corvinus]] of Hungary from 1463 to 1475 and was killed in battle in 1476 or 1477. Books about his cruelty were among the first bestsellers in German-speaking territories, and his patronymic is thought to have inspired the name of [[Count Dracula]] in [[Bram Stoker]]'s novel. Romanian tradition venerates him as a defender of Christendom.

Russian-born American pianist known for his virtuoso technique. Born in Kiev in the [[Russian Empire]] (present-day [[Ukraine]]), Horowitz studied at the Kiev Conservatory and toured during the [[Russian Civil War]], when he was often paid in food. He emigrated to Germany in 1925, intending not to return. His United States debut at Carnegie Hall in 1928 drew praise from Olin Downes of [[The New York Times]], who called his playing a "tornado unleashed from the steppes". He settled in the United States in 1939 and became a citizen in 1944, and he performed often with conductor [[Arturo Toscanini]]. He withdrew from public performance from 1953 to 1965. His television debut, a concert taped at Carnegie Hall, was broadcast nationwide by [[CBS]] in 1968.

Russian revolutionary and politician, first head of government of Soviet Russia (1917–1924). Lenin led the [[Bolsheviks]] in the [[October Revolution]], and his government withdrew from the First World War by signing a treaty conceding territory to the [[Central Powers]]. Opponents were suppressed in the Red Terror, in which tens of thousands were killed or interned. His administration defeated anti-Bolshevik armies in the [[Russian Civil War]] and oversaw the [[Polish–Soviet War]] of 1919–1921. In 1921 he introduced the New Economic Policy. Five non-Russian nations were forcibly reunited into the [[Soviet Union]] in 1922. Lenin died in Gorki, and [[Joseph Stalin]] succeeded him. Supporters regard him as a champion of revolutionary socialism, while critics accuse him of establishing a totalitarian dictatorship that oversaw mass killings.

Russian Futurist poet, playwright and artist. Born in [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] when it was part of the [[Russian Empire]], Mayakovsky co-signed the Futurist manifesto *A Slap in the Face of Public Taste* (1913). He wrote poems such as *A Cloud in Trousers* (1915), as well as plays and agitprop posters in support of the [[Bolsheviks]] during the [[Russian Civil War]]. Although his work supported the Bolshevik cause, his relationship with the Soviet state was often tumultuous, and works satirizing the Soviet system drew scorn from the state and literary establishment. He died by suicide. [[Joseph Stalin]] later praised him as the most talented poet of the Soviet era.

Russian and American novelist, poet, translator and entomologist. Nabokov wrote his first nine novels in Russian while living in Berlin, then began writing in English after moving to the United States. He taught Russian literature at [[Cornell University]] from 1948 to 1959. His novel *Lolita* (1955) ranked fourth on the Modern Library's list of the 100 best 20th-century novels in 1998, and his memoir *Speak, Memory* (1951) is considered among the greatest nonfiction works of the 20th century. He was also an expert lepidopterist and a composer of chess problems. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine wrote that his English style combined "Joycean word play" with a "Proustian evocation of mood and setting". He settled in Montreux, Switzerland, in 1961.

Russian politician and former [[KGB]] officer, president of Russia since 2012. He was prime minister from 1999 to 2000 and again from 2008 to 2012, and he served as president from 2000 to 2008. During his first presidency the economy grew on average by seven percent a year. In his third presidential term Russia annexed [[Crimea]] and supported a war in eastern Ukraine. In February 2022 he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which prompted international condemnation and expanded sanctions. In March 2023 the [[International Criminal Court]] issued an arrest warrant for him over war crimes related to the deportation of children. Critics argue his rule has been marked by corruption and human rights violations, and Russia has consistently received very low scores on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index and Freedom House's Freedom in the World index.

Russian principality (1125–1389), with its capital at Vladimir. It emerged during the disintegration of Kievan Rus', when Prince Yury Dolgoruky moved the capital from Rostov to Suzdal in 1125. His son Andrey moved it to Vladimir and had Kiev sacked in 1169, shifting political power to the northeast. After the Mongol invasions of 1237–1238 the princes submitted to Mongol rule. [[Alexander Nevsky]] was the last prince to reign directly in Vladimir. From 1331 the prince of [[Moscow]] was also grand prince of Vladimir, and by 1389 the two thrones were permanently united. The principality's territory later formed the core of the centralized Russian state.

Soviet singer-songwriter, poet and actor. His distinctive singing style and lyrics, with social and political commentary in often humorous street jargon, made him widely popular, although the official Soviet cultural establishment largely ignored his work. From 1964 he performed at Moscow's Taganka Theatre, where he played the title role in Yuri Lyubimov's 1971 production of *Hamlet*. He appeared in more than 25 films, often as rugged antiheroes or outcasts. His songs spread through clandestine tape recordings despite state censorship, and he wrote over 700 compositions. Official disapproval, including a 1973 Central Committee resolution condemning his underground performances, did not stop his popularity, and his death triggered mass public mourning.

Grand Prince of [[Kievan Rus']] from 978, canonized as a saint by the [[Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]]. Vladimir was the illegitimate youngest son of [[Sviatoslav I]] and his housekeeper Malusha. After a fratricidal war in which his brothers Yaropolk and Oleg died, he took Kiev in 978, and by 980 he had consolidated his realm to the [[Baltic Sea]]. He subdued the Vyatichi, Radimichi and Yatvingians and campaigned against the Volga Bulgars. Originally a follower of [[Slavic paganism]], he built a pagan temple in Kiev dedicated to six gods. He converted to [[Christianity]] in 988 and ordered mass baptism in Kiev, initiating the Christianization of the realm. While still a pagan, he had numerous wives and took eight hundred concubines.

Largest city and administrative center of Primorsky Krai, on the [[Sea of Japan]] (pop., 2021: 603,519). The city was founded in 1860 as a Russian military outpost, and in 1872 the main Russian naval base on the [[Pacific Ocean]] was transferred there. The name means "Lord of the East". In Mandarin Chinese it is known as Haishenwai, or "sea cucumber bay", for its historical abundance of [[Sea cucumber|sea cucumbers]]. White Russian and Allied forces occupied the city in 1918, Japanese forces remained until 1922, and the Red Army occupied it that same year. It became part of the Russian Federation after the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union]]. As the terminus of the [[Trans-Siberian Railway]], it is the largest Russian port on the Pacific and home to the headquarters of the Pacific Fleet.

Set of words in a language, or the set known to an individual. Vocabulary can be oral, written or signed, and it is typically divided into active vocabulary, the words used regularly, and passive vocabulary, the words recognized but seldom used. It is a central focus of [[Linguistics]], [[Psychology]] and [[Education]]. Vocabulary is not limited to single words, as it also includes collocations, idioms and other phraseology. Estimates of vocabulary size range from as high as 200 thousand to as low as 10 thousand, depending on the definition used. Acquiring an adequate vocabulary is one of the largest challenges in learning a second [[Language|language]]. In [[Semiotics|semiotics]], vocabulary refers to the complete set of symbols in a sign system.

Clear distilled [[Alcoholic beverage|alcoholic beverage]] composed mainly of water and [[Ethanol|ethanol]]. Its varieties originated in [[Poland]] and [[Russia]]. Traditionally it is made by distilling fermented cereal grains and potatoes, though some modern brands use [[Maize|maize]], sugar cane, fruit or honey. Standard vodkas have been 40% alcohol by volume since the 1890s, while the [[European Union]] sets a minimum of 37.5%. It is traditionally drunk neat and often served chilled in the so-called "vodka belt" of countries including Russia, Poland and Sweden. The English word is borrowed from Russian and literally means "little water". The earliest written mention of the word, in Polish court records, dates from 1405. Since the 1960s the unflavoured Swedish *brännvin* has also been called vodka.

American [[Fashion|fashion]] magazine, founded in New York in 1892 by Arthur Baldwin Turnure. It was originally a weekly aimed at the New York [[Upper class|upper class]], and Condé Nast bought it in 1909 and turned it into a women's magazine. Vogue became monthly in 1973, and from 2026 it publishes eight issues a year. [[Anna Wintour]] served as editor-in-chief of the American edition from 1988 to 2025, and Chloe Malle has overseen its editorial content since 2025. *British Vogue*, launched in 1916, was the first international edition, and there were 28 international editions as of March 2025. Critics have argued that the magazine's imagery has long favored slender body types and limited ethnic diversity.

Vast region of space between the filaments of the large-scale structure of the [[Universe|universe]], containing very few or no galaxies. Voids typically have a diameter of 10 to 100 [[Parsec|megaparsecs]] (30 to 300 million [[Light-year|light-years]]), and particularly large ones are called supervoids. Voids were first discovered in 1978 by Stephen Gregory and Laird A. Thompson at Kitt Peak National Observatory. They form through gravitational instability, as denser regions collapse under gravity and produce the foam-like cosmic web of voids and [[Galaxy|galaxy]] filaments seen today. Even the emptiest voids contain more than ~15% of the average matter density of the universe, so they look almost empty to an observer. Voids correlate with cooler regions of the [[Cosmic microwave background]] through the Sachs–Wolfe effect, which makes them significant evidence for [[Dark energy]].

Autonomous province in northern [[Serbia]] (pop., 2022: 1,749,356), covering 21,506 sq km. It comprises the historical regions of Bačka, Banat and Syrmia, north of the national capital [[Belgrade]] and the Sava and Danube rivers, and its administrative center is [[Novi Sad]]. Sirmium, now Sremska Mitrovica, was one of the four capitals of the [[Roman Empire]], and six [[Roman emperor|Roman emperors]] were born in or near it. Goths, Huns, Gepids and Avars ruled the area after the Romans, and [[Slavs]] settled it in the 6th and 7th centuries. The name derives from the Serbian Voivodeship, an Austrian province from 1849 to 1860. Serbs make up 68.4% of the population and Hungarians 10.5%. Its fertile plains make it an important agricultural region.

Small [[Rodent|rodent]] related to lemmings and hamsters, with about 155 [[Species|species]]. Voles grow to 8–23 cm (3–9 in), and most do not exceed 16 months of age in the wild. Litters of two to nine offspring are produced monthly during the breeding season, so populations can grow very large quickly. Voles eat small plants, and they can girdle small trees and ground cover. Many predators eat them, including [[Owl|owls]], [[Weasel|weasels]], [[Fox|foxes]] and [[Snake|snakes]].

River in [[Russia]], the longest in [[Europe]], flowing into the [[Caspian Sea]]. It is 3,531 km (2,194 mi) long and drains 1,360,000 sq km (530,000 sq mi), the largest drainage basin in Europe. It is also Europe's largest river by average discharge at its delta, between 8,000 and 8,500 cubic meters per second. Because it drains into the endorheic Caspian Sea, the Volga does not naturally connect to any ocean. Five of Russia's ten largest cities, including [[Moscow]], lie in its basin. The name derives from a Proto-Slavic word meaning "wetness", and [[Turkic peoples|Turkic peoples]] formerly called it Itil. Russian literature often calls it "Volga-Matushka" (Mother Volga).

Medieval Bulgar state around the confluence of the [[Volga]] and Kama rivers in what is now European [[Russia]], existing between the 9th and 13th centuries. The Bulgars, an Oghuric people, had come under the overlordship of the [[Khazars]], and the state gained independence after Khazaria was destroyed by [[Sviatoslav I]] in the late 10th century. Volga Bulgaria adopted [[Islam]] as its state religion in 922, 66 years before the Christianization of Kievan Rus'. Its capital, Bolghar, lay about 160 km south of modern [[Kazan]]. The state dominated trade on the Volga, exchanging northern furs and slaves for silks, spices and metals, and it minted silver dirhams. Mongol forces under Batu Khan razed major cities in 1236–1237, and the remnants were integrated into the [[Golden Horde]].
